outcome: Nothing has settled or moved this bullet since 26 January 2024: no source found identifies a first-order theory whose universality spectrum is minimum, or shows that none exists. The events found are pre-window (Kojman and Shelah 1992; Shelah SH1164, 2021, which only expects T_ceq to be minimal and proves a restricted non-existence result) or post-window papers on neighbouring questions (Freitag and Mutchnik on stable forking, 31 Aug 2026; Zhang on the generalised Gaifman conjecture, 17 Aug 2026), each recorded below and each discounted as a different question.
problem_asks: Statement (Wikipedia, Model theory and formal languages, Jan 2024 wording): 'The universality spectrum problem: Is there a first-order theory whose universality spectrum is minimum?' Unpacked: (1) a first-order theory T; the universality-spectrum literature works with complete theories, and the bullet's wording does not say otherwise. (2) The universality spectrum of T, USP(T), the set of cardinals lambda in which T has a universal model (the literature also uses variants). (3) 'Minimum': a least element among universality spectra under an ordering the bullet does not name; the literature's ordering is Shelah's <=univ (the wording in SH1164 is 'under <=univ'). (4) The question is existential: it asks for one theory T that is minimum. Its answer is either a witness theory or a proof that no theory is minimum. It asks for no bounds, no cardinal arithmetic hypotheses, no classification, and no comparison class other than the ordering in (3). A theory that is minimum only among the stable unsuperstable theories, or only among non-simple theories, does not answer part (4) as worded.

events.what_happened: Menachem Kojman and Saharon Shelah, 'The universality spectrum of stable unsuperstable theories', arXiv math/9201253 (submitted 15 Jan 1992), published Ann. Pure Appl. Logic 58 (1992) 57-72 (report number KjSh:447). For a complete theory T that is stable but not superstable, it proves non-existence of universal models in certain cardinals under cardinal-arithmetic hypotheses, e.g. no universal model in aleph_omega when aleph_omega < 2^aleph_0, generalised from aleph_0 to kappa = cf(kappa) < kappa(T). The introduction, seen only in a search snippet and not read in full, calls a specific 'canonical' stable unsuperstable theory minimal: if any stable unsuperstable theory has a universal model in some cardinality, the canonical one does too.
events.delivers: Restricted to stable, not superstable, theories: non-existence of universal models in listed cardinals under stated hypotheses. The 'canonical theory is minimal' claim, per the snippet, is minimality within the stable unsuperstable class only. It says nothing about a minimum over all first-order theories.
events.remains: All of problem_asks. No theory is shown minimum among all first-order theories, and no theory is shown to have no minimum.

checked_by.qualification: Peer-reviewed journal of record in mathematical logic
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted and published the paper, Ann. Pure Appl. Logic 58 (1992) 57-72

events.direction: Cuts against universal models for stable unsuperstable theories in the listed cardinals. For this bullet it is neutral: it bounds one class of theories and does not locate a minimum.

events.what_happened: Saharon Shelah, 'Universality: new criterion for non-existence', arXiv 2108.06727 (report Sh:1164), v1 15 Aug 2021, v2 14 Mar 2022; published Boll. Unione Mat. Ital. 16 (2023) 43-64 after a referee report (arXiv comment: '24 pages, after referee report'). It gives new sufficient conditions under which the class of models of T_ceq (an equivalence relation with a family of choice functions; not simple, but 'very low among the non-simple' theories per the abstract) has no universal model in a given cardinal lambda. The introduction says T_ceq is 'a proto-typical minimal non-simple T, so are expecting it (under <=univ) to be low'. That is stated as an expectation, not a theorem. The paper also poses open Question 0.1: does section 1 apply to more theories than section 2, and can the dividing line be characterised as simple versus non-simple?
events.revisions: v2 14 Mar 2022 (current on arXiv); journal version Boll. UMI 16 (2023) 43-64 after referee report.
events.delivers: Non-existence of universal models for the T_ceq model class in cardinals lambda meeting the paper's conditions. That is a restricted result on one theory's models, not a minimality result. It names T_ceq as the candidate the author expects to be minimal among non-simple theories under the universality ordering, but proves no minimality, and does not show whether any first-order theory has a minimum universality spectrum.
events.remains: Whether any complete first-order theory has a minimum universality spectrum; whether T_ceq is minimum (only expected in the paper); the simple versus non-simple dividing line (Question 0.1).

events.what_happened: Saharon Shelah, 'No universal group in a cardinal', arXiv 1311.4997 (report Sh:1029). Versions: v1 20 Nov 2013; v2 23 Apr 2014; v3 6 Sep 2021; v4 23 Aug 2023; v5 28 Jan 2024; v6 4 Mar 2026 (comment: 'Minor proofreading'). It studies when a universal member exists in a cardinal lambda = 2^{<lambda}; for linear orders none exists when lambda is regular and far from GCH. It introduces the 'olive property', a sufficient condition for no universal member that is not covered by earlier results and falls outside SOP_4, and shows the class of groups has it.
events.revisions: v2 23 Apr 2014; v3 6 Sep 2021; v4 23 Aug 2023; v5 28 Jan 2024 (two days after the frozen revision); v6 4 Mar 2026 ('minor proofreading'). The author's site, shelah.logic.at/papers/1029/, is said to be more up to date.
events.delivers: Non-existence of universal members for classes of structures (linear orders, groups) in cardinals of the form lambda = 2^{<lambda}, under the olive property. It is restricted to those classes and cardinals. From the abstract, it does not identify or exclude a minimum universality spectrum among first-order theories.
events.time_since_posted: about 12 years 11 months (v1 Nov 2013); v6 posted Mar 2026
events.direction: Adds non-existence sufficient conditions for classes of structures. Neutral for the minimum question as worded.

events.what_happened: Scott Mutchnik, 'On NSOP_2 theories', arXiv 2206.08512. Abstract: 'Answering a question of Džamonja and Shelah, we show that every NSOP_2 theory is NSOP_1.' Search snippets say it appeared in J. Eur. Math. Soc. 28 (2026), no. 8, pp. 3475-3498 (DOI 10.4171/JEMS/1679); the journal page itself was not opened. The Džamonja-Shelah question concerns maximality in the order ◁* (tied to Keisler's order), not universal models or spectra.
events.revisions: v2 1 Jul 2022; v3 28 Sep 2022; v4 14 Jun 2023 (current on arXiv). Journal publication in JEMS 2026 per search snippet.
events.delivers: Every NSOP_2 theory is NSOP_1: a dividing-line result between two NSOP classes. It does not concern universal models, universality spectra, or a minimum.

events.what_happened: James Freitag and Scott Mutchnik, 'A counterexample to the stable forking conjecture', arXiv 2609.00436 (math.LO), v1 submitted 31 Aug 2026, one version. The abstract: 'Using ChatGPT 5.6, we find a counterexample to the stable forking conjecture. This answers a long-standing open question of Hart, Kim and Pillay (1996).' Section 1.1 says 'This is an AI-generated result proven with the help of GPT-5.6 Sol.' A secondary source (aiweekly.co) describes the counterexample as the theory of an infinite-dimensional vector space over the division ring of fractions of the quantum graph algebra of the random graph. That source is not the paper. The conjecture concerns forking in simple theories, not universality spectra.
events.delivers: A claimed, unrefereed counterexample to the stable forking conjecture, which asks whether forking in simple theories is witnessed by stable formulas. It bears on no universality spectrum and does not touch the minimum question.
events.time_since_posted: about 6 weeks (posted 31 Aug 2026, record date 13 Oct 2026)
events.directly_checkable: The counterexample is a theory, not a finite object, so it is not directly checkable by hand from what I read.
events.doubts: Unrefereed. Its AI credit is worded two ways: 'ChatGPT 5.6' (abstract) and 'GPT-5.6 Sol' (Section 1.1). The trackers I found report no independent specialist assessment, and a search summary reports that MathWorld noted no independent verification as of 7 Sep 2026 (MathWorld page not opened). I found no expert commentary up to 13 Oct 2026.
events.direction: If correct, a negative answer to the stable forking conjecture. That is a different question from this bullet.
events.object: Per aiweekly.co (secondary, not the paper), the theory of an infinite-dimensional vector space over the division ring of fractions of the quantum graph algebra of the random graph, a simple theory whose forking is not witnessed by stable formulas. I could not confirm this construction in the arXiv text I read (abstract and Section 1.1).

A footnote says the arguments 'were based on proofs generated using JF's ChatGPT account'. The authors say the proofs of the relevant facts and some aspects of the setup were 'written entirely by the authors', and that 'no AI tool was used in the actual writing of this manuscript'. events.what_happened: Yi Zhang, 'Counterexamples to the Generalized Gaifman Conjecture', arXiv 2608.16099 (math.LO), submitted 17 Aug 2026, one version. Abstract: 'Shelah and Usvyatsov proposed the Generalized Gaifman Conjecture [SU25, Conjecture 1.1]. We give a negative answer.' The Gaifman property concerns a theory with a distinguished unary predicate P: every model of Th(P) is the P-part of a model of T. A search summary (emergentmind, not the paper) says the counterexamples give far fewer than 2^kappa extensions, including 0 or exactly kappa extensions over suitable bases. The paper does not mention universal models or universality spectra.
events.delivers: Negative answer to a generalised conjecture about the Gaifman property and extension counts over a predicate. It is a different question from the universality spectrum and does not touch the minimum question.
events.doubts: Single author, unrefereed. The PDF text was not readable through my tool, so the counterexamples are checked only at the level of the abstract and the HTML version's disclosure section. The extension counts come from a search summary, not the paper text I read.
events.direction: Negative answer to a generalised Gaifman conjecture. Neighbouring model theory, not this question.
events.object: Per the emergentmind summary (not read in the paper): constructions in which failure of the Gaifman property gives 0 or exactly kappa extensions over suitable bases, one example adding one element to an equivalence-relation structure. Unverified.

summary: The bullet, as the Wikipedia list gives it in the Model theory and formal languages section, reads: 'The universality spectrum problem: Is there a first-order theory whose universality spectrum is minimum?' The only substantive literature on the notion is Shelah's programme, and I found no event since 26 January 2024 that bears on whether a minimum exists. The closest work is Shelah's SH1164 (arXiv 2108.06727, Aug 2021; Boll. UMI 2023). It names T_ceq (an equivalence relation with a family of choice functions) as a 'proto-typical minimal non-simple T' and expects it to be low under the universality ordering. That is an expectation in the paper, not a theorem, and it is pre-window. The 1992 Kojman-Shelah paper shows non-existence of universal models for stable unsuperstable theories under cardinal hypotheses; a search snippet of its introduction calls one canonical stable unsuperstable theory minimal within that class. I read the abstract only and did not check that claim in the text. A reader who takes 'minimum' relative to the stable unsuperstable class could count it, but the bullet asks about all first-order theories, so I do not count it as an answer. The SH1029 paper (arXiv 1311.4997) adds the olive property and non-existence for groups; it is restricted to classes of structures and does not address minimality of spectra for theories. Mutchnik's NSOP_2 result (2022; JEMS 2026 per a snippet) answers a Džamonja-Shelah maximality question, not this one. Two 2026 AI-credited model-theory papers are post-window: Freitag and Mutchnik (arXiv 2609.00436, 31 Aug 2026), which credit ChatGPT 5.6 (called GPT-5.6 Sol in Section 1.1) with a counterexample to the stable forking conjecture, and Zhang (arXiv 2608.16099, 17 Aug 2026), which gives a negative answer to the generalised Gaifman conjecture and says the author found the proof with the assistance of ChatGPT. Both concern different conjectures. Neither bears on universality spectra, so the bullet has no AI-credited event. The follow-up that SH1164 cites ('Shelah et al., in preparation') is listed by the Hebrew University record as Sh:F2150. The arXiv abstract page, as read by my fetch tool, gave Sh:F2071 for the same reference, which I could not confirm, and the ar5iv text says only '[S+]'. I treat Sh:F2150 as the better-supported number, because the HUJI record is the explicit source. I found no arXiv, journal or talk record for either number. On the AI side I searched for the problem's name with AI terms, for model-theory AI results, and for the known AI-result trackers (Erdős problems, OpenAI's May 2026 unit-distance counterexample, kingy.ai, aiweekly.co). None of these touched universality spectra. The OpenAI unit-distance result is combinatorial geometry, so it is outside this bullet. The ambiguity I could not resolve is whether Shelah's 1992 'canonical theory is minimal' and the 2021 expectation about T_ceq should count as partial progress under a restricted reading of 'minimum'. On the wording as given, I say no. Neither gives a theory that is minimum among all theories, and neither proves that none is.
competing_reading: A reader could treat Shelah's 2021 expectation that T_ceq is minimal among non-simple theories, together with the 1992 Kojman-Shelah minimality of a canonical stable unsuperstable theory, as partial progress on the bullet: each identifies a candidate theory minimal in a class. Against that: both are either pre-window or only an expectation, and the bullet asks for a minimum among all first-order theories under the literature's ordering. Neither result gives such a minimum or excludes one.
what_would_settle_it: (a) A paper, post-window, proving that some complete first-order theory (T_ceq or another) has a universality spectrum that is least under <=univ, or proving that no theory does. (b) Reading the text of Shelah's 'Divide and Conquer' (Theoria 2021) to confirm how the survey poses the question and which ordering 'minimum' refers to; I could not read its text. (c) Confirming the Sh:F2150 follow-up (Shelah et al.), or finding a preprint with that number, since it is the work SH1164 says will continue the minimality question. (d) A citation index (Google Scholar, MathSciNet or zbMATH) listing post-2024 papers that cite SH1164 or the 1992 paper.
